source_text: Τί τοίνυν ἦν τὸ προτρεψάμενον αὐτὸν εἰς φυγὴν καὶ ποιῆσαν ἀπαυτομολῆσαι τοῦ διδασκάλου, τῆς ἱκετείας. τῆς ἐλπίδος, τῆς ζωῆς, τῶν προπεπονημένων; »πώλησον τὰ ὑπάρχοντά σου.« τί δὲ τοῦτό ἐστιν; οὐχ ὃ προχείρως δέχονταί τινες, τὴν ὑπάρχουσαν οὐσίαν ἀπορρῖψαι προστάσσει καὶ ἀποστῆναι τῶν χρημάτων, ἀλλὰ τὰ δόγματα τὰ περὶ χρημάτων ἐξορίσαι τῆς ψυχῆς, τὴν πρὸς αὐτὰ συμπάθειαν. τὴν ὑπεράγαν ἐπιθυμίαν, τὴν περὶ αὐτὰ πτοίαν καὶ νόσον, τὰς μερίμνας, τὰς ἀκάνθας τοῦ βίου, αἳ τὸ σπέρμα τῆς ζωῆς συμπνίγουσιν. οὔτε γὰρ μέγα καὶ ζηλωτὸν τὸ τηνάλλως ἀπορεῖν χρημάτων μὴ οὐκ ἐπὶ λόγῳ ζωῆς (οὕτω μέν γ᾿ ἂν ἦσαν οἱ μηδὲν ἔχοντες μηδαμῇ, ἀλλὰ ἔρημοι καὶ μεταῖται τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἡμέραν, οἱ κατὰ τὰς ὁδοὺς ἐρριμμένοι πτωχοί, »ἀγνοοῦντες« δὲ θεὸν καὶ »δικαιοσύνην θεοῦ«, κατ᾿ αὐτὸ μόνον τὸ ἄκρως ἀπορεῖν καὶ ἀμηχανεῖν βίου καὶ τῶν ἐλαχίστων σπανίζειν μακαριώτατοι καὶ θεοφιλέστατοι καὶ μόνοι ζωὴν ἔχοντες αἰώνιον) οὔτε καινὸν τὸ ἀπείπασθαι πλοῦτον καὶ χαρίσασθαι πτωχοῖς ἢ πατρίσιν, ὃ πολλοὶ πρὸ τῆς τοῦ σωτῆρος καθόδου πεποιήκασιν, οἳ μὲν τῆς εἰς λόγους σχολῆς καὶ νεκρᾶς σοφίας ἕνεκεν. οἵ δὲ φήμης κενῆς καὶ κενοδοξίας, Ἀναξαγόραι καὶ Δημόκριτοι καὶ Κράτητες.
thought_title: What the command to sell really means
orientation: Clement is explaining what Jesus' command to the rich man to sell his possessions actually required, arguing it was not outward poverty but the removal of inner attachments.
pass_a_gloss: What then was the thing that urged him to flight and made him desert the teacher, the supplication, the hope, the life, the things previously labored for? "Sell your possessions." But what is this? It is not what some readily take it to be: he does not command him to throw away the substance that belongs to him and to stand apart from money, but to banish from the soul the opinions about money, the sympathy toward them, the excessive desire, the excitement and sickness about them, the cares, the thorns of life, which choke the seed of life. For neither is it great and enviable to be without money in vain, not for the sake of the word of life (for in that case those who have nothing at all, but are destitute and beggars for the day, the poor persons thrown along the roads, but "ignorant" of God and "the righteousness of God," would by this very thing alone—the extreme lack and helplessness of life and the want of the smallest things—be most blessed and most beloved by God and the only ones having eternal life), nor is it new to renounce wealth and give it to poor persons or to fatherlands, which many did before the coming of the Savior, some for the sake of leisure for words and dead wisdom, others for empty fame and vainglory—Anaxagoras and Democritus and Crates.

choices.why: The glossary reserves 'possessions' for κτήματα, but here the verb ὑπάρχω in the neuter plural means what belongs to someone; 'possessions' is the natural English for the command being quoted.

choices.english: the substance that belongs to him
choices.why: οὐσία means substance or estate; rendering it as 'substance' keeps the philosophical register Clement uses, and the participle makes clear it is his own.
δόγματα here are the soul's settled judgments or beliefs about money, not official teachings; 'opinions' captures the inner cognitive attachment Clement wants expelled.
συμπάθεια is the felt affinity or fellow-feeling with money; 'sympathy' preserves the Stoic technical sense of an emotional bond to externals.

choices.term: τὴν περὶ αὐτὰ πτοίαν καὶ νόσον
choices.english: the excitement and sickness about them
choices.why: πτοία is a fluttering agitation or startled excitement, and νόσος is disease; both are standard Stoic terms for passions, so literal renderings keep the philosophical force.
This echoes the parable of the sower, where thorns choke the word; 'thorns of life' keeps the agricultural metaphor and the Gospel allusion.

bible_refs.note: αἳ τὸ σπέρμα τῆς ζωῆς συμπνίγουσιν, echoing the thorns that choke the seed
ἀγνοοῦντες δὲ θεὸν καὶ δικαιοσύνην θεοῦ

pass_b_english: What was it, then, that urged him to flee and made him desert the teacher, the supplication, the hope, the life, the labors he had already undertaken? "Sell your possessions" (Mark 10:21). And what does this mean? It is not what some hastily take it to be, a command to throw away the substance that belongs to him and to part with his money. Rather, it means expelling from the soul the opinions about money, the attachment to it, the excessive desire for it, the excitement and sickness about it, the cares, the thorns of life that choke the seed of life (Matthew 13:22). For it is no great and enviable thing to be without money for no reason, if it is not for the sake of life. If it were, then those who have nothing at all anywhere, poor persons and beggars who live from day to day, poor persons cast along the roads, who do not know God and the righteousness of God (Romans 10:3), would be, by the bare fact of their extreme lack and helplessness and want of even the smallest things, the most blessed and most beloved of God, and the only ones who have eternal life. Nor is it a new thing to renounce wealth and give it to poor people or to one's country. Many did this before the Savior's coming, some for the sake of leisure for words and dead wisdom, others for empty fame and vainglory: the Anaxagorases, the Democrituses, the Cratetes.
